description_full: Tenaris S.A., together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and supplies steel pipe products and related services for the energy industry and other industrial applications in North America, South America, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It provides steel casings to sustain the walls of oil and gas wells during and after drilling; steel tubing for conducting crude oil and natural gas to the surface after drilling has been completed; steel line pipes to transport crude oil and natural gas from wells to refineries, storage tanks, and loading and distribution centers; and mechanical and structural pipes for the transportation of other forms of gas and liquids under high pressure. The company also offers cold-drawn pipes for use in boilers, superheaters, condensers, heat exchangers, automobile production, and other industrial applications; premium joints and couplings for use in high temperature or high pressure environments under the TenarisHydril brand name; coiled tubing is used for oil and gas drilling and well workovers and for subsea pipelines; sucker rods used in oil extraction activities, tubes used for plumbing and construction applications, and oilfield / hydraulic fracturing services; pipe coating services; and automotive components. In addition, it engages in the sale of energy and raw materials; development, management, and licensing of intellectual property; procurement and trading services; and financial operations, as well as markets steel products. Further, the company manufactures and markets connections; and welded and seamless steel pipes. Tenaris S.A. was incorporated in 2001 and is based in Luxembourg, Luxembourg. Tenaris S.A. operates as a subsidiary of Techint Holdings S.àr.l.

financial_summary: Tenaris S.A. is a large-cap energy business with a $28.6B market cap on $12.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 8% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 33%.

The business throws off $2.0B in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 49× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 8.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin is roughly in line with the Energy median (16%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 53% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.72, it is more defensive than the market.
About $58.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The stock trades 41% below its DCF fair value of $95.66, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $33.32 to $290 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Energy peers: EV/EBITDA 20.1 vs 6.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 54% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $68.48 on average, 21% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.2%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.02).
It runs a 33% gross margin and converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.32x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $572.3M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.6% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 36%).
At current returns, reinvesting 4% of profits supports about 0.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 17.7% on average.
Analysts expect 13.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 7%.
It returns 8.0% a year to shareholders (4.8% in buybacks and 4.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 60.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 24,875 employees, each generates about $482K of revenue, 0.2x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 10.8% a year across its filed history.
